findings.headline: The council reports no operational breaches of TMSS limits during the period
findings.detail: The paper says the council complied with its prudential indicators and the limits in the 2026-27 treasury strategy, which had no in-year changes.
findings.matters: The council confirms its prudential indicators were met, which is the compliance position other councils and lenders check against the same code.
findings.figures: no operational breaches; no in-year TMSS changes
findings.quote: There were no operational breaches of the limits set in the TMSS during the period.

findings.headline: Investments achieved an average return of 3.73%, matching the SONIA target of 3.73%
findings.detail: The paper says the investment balance ranged between £13.1m and £41.0m, with an average of £29m and a weighted average maturity of 8 days. Investment income for the first half of the year was £0.538m.
findings.matters: A council holding short-term deposits and matching its benchmark return gives a comparison point for peers managing cash balances against SONIA.
findings.figures: 3.73% average return; SONIA target 3.73%; investment balances £13.1m to £41.0m; average £29m; £0.538m income in H1
findings.quote: During the period our target rate of SONIA was 3.73%. We matched the benchmark (achieving an average return of 3.73%).

findings.headline: The 10-year gilt yield rose from 4.4% in late February to above 5.4% by period end
findings.detail: The paper says the gilt rise added demand to the short-term LA lending market, and that spreads widened to occasionally above PWLB. It notes the margins are applied on top of gilt rates to reach the council's borrowing rate.
findings.matters: A rising gilt yield feeds straight into PWLB and LA lending costs, so finance officers at peer councils will read the movement as a direct input to their own borrowing costs.
findings.figures: 10-year gilt 4.4% late February 2026; 5.2% in May; above 5.4% at period end; PWLB margin typically 0.8% for NELC
findings.quote: The yield on the key 10-year gilt rose from 4.4% in late February just prior to attacks on Iran commencing to 5.2% in May

findings.headline: A 90% support payment is cited as the reason for stacking temporary loans into December to cover SEND deficits
findings.detail: The paper says the temporary loans will run off as soon as the support funds are received. It also describes the local authority lending market as under stress from SEND deficit funding across the country.
findings.matters: Councils funding SEND deficit gaps through temporary borrowing are a pressure that finance directors and lenders are tracking across the sector.
findings.figures: 90% support payment expected Q3; temporary loans into December
findings.quote: we stacked a corresponding amount of temporary loans into December

findings.headline: Council is under-borrowed by £61.0m against its capital financing requirement at 30/09/2026
findings.detail: The paper says the under-borrowed position is typical for similar authorities but represents increased interest rate risk. Cash balances are used in place of external borrowing as an interim measure.
findings.matters: The size of the gap between borrowing and CFR is the unfunded capital the council must still finance, and a peer reader will compare it with their own under-borrowing.
findings.figures: CFR £248.7m estimated at 30/09/2026; over/(under) borrowing (£61.0m); £236.5m estimated CFR at 31/03/2026
findings.quote: Over / (under) borrowing (£58.4m) (£61.0m)

findings.headline: Capital expenditure for 2026-27 is forecast at £111.0m, down £19.9m from the original £130.9m budget
findings.detail: The paper shows the reduction in the draft outturn, with borrowing requirement reduced by £15.8m and grant funding reduced by £4.0m.
findings.matters: A £19.9m reduction in the in-year capital programme drives the lower borrowing need, which is the link a finance director elsewhere will follow.
findings.figures: £130.9m original 2026-27 budget; £111.0m 2026-27 draft outturn; -£19.9m change; £42.9m borrowing outturn
findings.quote: Total Expenditure 130.9 -19.9 111.0 85.0 47.9

findings.headline: Council expects to borrow up to £71m over the next few years and £80m to replace maturing loans, with a peak requirement of £151m of new loans by the end of 2028-29
findings.detail: The paper links the new borrowing to a rising capital financing requirement and the need to refinance maturing debt. It states the liability benchmark is the basis for assessing future borrowing decisions.
findings.matters: The scale of future new and replacement borrowing is a funding requirement that lenders and other councils would want to see.
findings.figures: up to £71m new borrowing over the next few years; £80m replacement of maturing loans; peak requirement of £151m new loans by end 2028-29
findings.quote: will therefore need to borrow up to £71m over the next few years. A further £80m will be required to replace maturing loans.

findings.headline: The council took two PWLB loans at 5.40% and 5.42%, each £5m and maturing in 2028
findings.detail: The two PWLB loans were taken in September 2026, with the rates given in the table of loans arranged during the period. The paper describes PWLB rates as close to 30-year highs.
findings.matters: These are recent PWLB rates from a named council, which shows the cost of long-term funding in the current market and is directly comparable to what other councils are paying.

findings.headline: The council arranged £73.5m of new short-term loans as rates rose, while deferring long-term borrowing
findings.detail: The paper says the loans were taken from several start dates over periods of up to a year to meet cash flow needs. It later adds that the council will now meet cash flow needs through new borrowing with lower balances, with a mix of short and long-term loans.
findings.matters: A council shifting from deferral to new borrowing, and from LA short-term lenders to a mix, is a change in funding approach that lenders and peers will follow.
findings.figures: £73.5m new loans in the period; loans of up to one year
findings.quote: As interest rates rose, we arranged £73.5m of new loans over several start dates and periods of up to a year

findings.headline: Higher investment returns generated £0.4m of surplus income above budget in the period, and an underspend on borrowing provided a further £1.3m
findings.detail: The paper states both sums are available to fund services. The investment income figure is the surplus above budget.
findings.matters: Treasury income and borrowing underspends being redirected to services is a source of in-year budget flexibility that other councils may be tracking.
findings.figures: £0.4m surplus investment income above budget; £1.3m borrowing underspend for distribution
findings.quote: Higher investment returns, even with our cautious approach, has generated surplus income (above budget) of £0.4m during the period

findings.headline: Borrowing costs are projected to exceed 10% of overall net budgets by the end of the current MTFP period
findings.detail: The paper says this affects affordability, and that capital plans may need adjusting if rates stay elevated. It notes some capacity exists in the current programme to re-profile spend without removing schemes.
findings.matters: It is a stated intention to re-profile capital in response to rates, which other councils with similar 10% limits will be weighing.
findings.figures: 10% of overall net budgets; MTFP period end
findings.quote: Borrowing costs are expected to rise going forward and are now projected to be above 10% of overall Net Budgets by the end of the current MTFP period.

findings.headline: Financing costs as a share of net revenue stream are revised to 7.76% for 2026-27 against an original 8.47%, and projected at 9.74% for 2027-28 and 10.51% for 2028-29
findings.detail: The paper says the 2026-27 ratio came in below projections, due to capital reprofiling and short-term lenders offering lower rates. Future years are affected by higher long-term rate expectations, and the paper states the final year exceeds the council's 10% voluntary limit.
findings.matters: A council's own 10% affordability ceiling, and the path towards it, is the measure a finance director must defend in budget setting, and a lender can read how far the projections move against it.
findings.figures: General Fund financing cost ratio: 8.47% original 2026-27, 7.76% revised 2026-27, 9.74% 2027-28, 10.51% 2028-29; 10% prudent limit

findings.headline: Treasury is on course to deliver an outturn £2.2m below the original 2026-27 budget
findings.detail: The paper gives the treasury outturn against budget and links it to investment returns above budget and an underspend on borrowing costs.
findings.matters: It shows the in-year treasury position against budget, which finance officers elsewhere can weigh against their own treasury variances.
findings.figures: £2.2m below original 2026-27 budget
findings.quote: Overall Treasury is on course to deliver an outturn position £2.2m below the original 2026-27 budget.

findings.headline: Council borrowing at 30/09/2026 is £187.7m, with the year-end forecast revised to £205.6m against an original estimate of £226.4m
findings.detail: The paper attributes the lower forecast mainly to slippage in the capital programme, partly offset by temporary borrowing to fund SEND deficits. Borrowing rose £9m in the period.
findings.matters: A finance director at a peer council can compare how a £20.8m fall in forecast borrowing, driven by capital slippage, sits against their own year-end debt projection.
findings.figures: £187.7m at 30/09/2026; £205.6m revised year-end forecast; £226.4m original forecast
findings.quote: Actual borrowing at period end stood at £187.7m and the revised year end forecast is £205.6m.

findings.headline: The Corporation Road Bridge governance working group has not yet convened, and its first task is to set its terms of reference.
findings.detail: The Monitoring Officer said there were no new developments on governance or risk. An update on the project's critical path is to be given to scrutiny in September, and commercial sensitivities may limit transparency.
findings.matters: A capital scheme whose governance review has not yet started, and whose critical path will next be reported in September, is one that a lender or peer finance director would want to track.
findings.quote: It was noted that this still needed to take place.

findings.headline: Two Priority 1 internal audit findings, on homelessness and car parking enforcement, were discussed, with the car parking Priority 1 status described as ongoing.
findings.detail: A member asked for more detail on the action plans and potential service impacts. Officers said delays to Section 38 expenditure audits were caused by reprioritisation of other audits, not a lack of resources.
findings.matters: Open Priority 1 findings in revenue-facing services are a control issue that finance directors elsewhere will recognise as a signal to test their own enforcement and homelessness spend.
findings.figures: two Priority 1 findings
findings.quote: ongoing Priority 1 status

findings.headline: Internal audit's current overall assurance rating is "satisfactory assurance", with "substantial assurance" as the aspiration.
findings.detail: The committee briefly discussed moving from the current rating to the higher level and the practicality of achieving it across all areas. The annual internal audit report and opinion was noted.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders use the internal audit opinion as a signal of control quality, and this paper records the council's current rating and its stated target.
findings.quote: the aspiration for "substantial assurance" versus the current "satisfactory assurance"

findings.headline: Members raised a recurring trend of mid-year forecast overspends consistently reducing by year-end.
findings.detail: A member questioned the accuracy of initial overspend forecasts. The Head of Finance said forecasts rely mainly on service directors' predictions, particularly in demand-led services such as Children's and Adults' Social Care, and that finance provides challenge and support.
findings.matters: Forecast accuracy in demand-led social care is a question that finance directors across English councils face when setting mid-year budget expectations.
findings.quote: A member raised a recurring trend of forecasted overspends at mid -year consistently reducing by year -end

findings.headline: External audit work on the 2024/25 accounts is on track to meet the November deadline for completion.
findings.detail: The external auditors reported that materiality levels have been set and risk assessments are being finalised. The committee noted the strategy memorandum.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or elsewhere, will want to know whether the audit of the 2024/25 accounts is on schedule for the November deadline.
findings.quote: It was confirmed that external audit work was on track to meet the November deadline for completion.

findings.headline: The cost of local government reorganisation is reported at £1 million, noted under the treasury outturn item.
findings.detail: The committee noted the cost of £1 million related to local government reorganization during its consideration of the 2025/26 treasury outturn report. The paper gives no further breakdown of the cost.
findings.matters: A one-off reorganisation cost of this size is a funding question that finance directors at councils facing similar change will need to plan for.
findings.figures: £1 million
findings.quote: The cost of £1 million related to local government reorganization was noted.

findings.headline: The 2025/26 treasury outturn report records that the council assesses borrowing needs daily and does not actively manage capital projects to slow borrowing.
findings.detail: In response to a query on the treasury outturn report, officers said borrowing need is assessed every day. The committee noted the report without further comment.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare this approach to daily borrowing-need assessment with their own practice on phasing capital spend against borrowing.
findings.quote: does not actively manage capital projects to slow borrowing

findings.headline: Two advisory audits on the Freeport Company are ongoing ahead of accountable responsibilities transferring from NELC to the Hull and East Yorkshire Combined Authority.
findings.detail: The paper lists the advisory work as part of audit support to the Council, in preparation for the transfer of accountable responsibilities. It does not give a transfer date in this document.
findings.matters: A change of accountable body for a Freeport moves responsibility for its funds and controls to another authority, which finance officers at other councils and lenders to the Freeport would want to know about.
findings.figures: 2 advisory audits (ongoing)
findings.quote: in preparation for the transfer of Accountable responsibilities from NELC to the Hull and East Yorkshire Combined Authority

findings.headline: Internal audit had delivered 330 days against a target of 310 days at 30 September 2026, within a plan of 930 days to 31 May 2027.
findings.detail: The paper reports 38 days of the 120-day contingency still available. It also says that completing the 2025/26 outstanding audits needed more resource than anticipated, leaving residual risk to delivery that will be monitored and may require re-prioritisation of the plan.
findings.matters: Whether an audit plan is ahead of or behind its days target, and how much contingency is left, shows whether assurance for the year-end opinion is on track.
findings.figures: 330 days delivered against a target of 310 days; 930 days planned to 31 May 2027 including 120 days contingency; 38 contingency days remaining
findings.quote: As of 30 September 2026, 330 days had been delivered compared to the target of 310 days at this point in the audit cycle

findings.headline: Overdue internal audit actions for 2025/26 stood at 17 of 133 as of 30 September 2026, against 2 of 137 for 2024/25 and 1 of 144 for 2023/24.
findings.detail: Table 3 shows managers had confirmed 63 of the 2025/26 actions as implemented, with 41 not yet due and 9 with amended dates. The paper's table records 3 risk-accepted actions for 2025/26.
findings.matters: A rise in overdue management actions from one year's audit cycle to the next is a governance signal that peers and lenders can compare against their own action-tracking records.
findings.figures: 2025/26: 17 overdue of 133 total actions; 2024/25: 2 overdue of 137; 2023/24: 1 overdue of 144
findings.quote: Overdue  1 2 17

findings.headline: Internal audit gave Limited Assurance to one of the five 2026/27 audits issued in final up to 30 September 2026, the Community Assets report.
findings.detail: The report says management has introduced control improvements and acted on lease and rent review backlogs and arrears, but these measures had only recently been implemented, so there was insufficient evidence they have reduced the rent review backlogs. The text names the report Community Assets, while Appendix 1 lists the Limited report as Commercial Estates.
findings.matters: A Limited Assurance opinion on rent review backlogs and arrears in a council's property income area is an audit weakness that a finance director, or a lender assessing income controls, would want to track to closure.
findings.figures: 1 of 5 audits issued in final rated Limited (Table 2); Appendix 1 shows 0 Priority 1, 1 Priority 2 and 2 Priority 3 actions for this report
findings.quote: One report, Community Assets, received Limited Assurance.

findings.paper_title: 11. Audit and Governance report Statutory Intervention
findings.headline: Considerable officer time and financial resource already invested in the emerging Local Plan, with the Minister identifying a risk of waste; no amount given
findings.detail: The report says the Minister identified the risk that not progressing the Plan would waste the accumulated time, effort and investment. It refers to the wider financial consequences of the Local Plan programme being managed through the existing budgetary and programme arrangements.
findings.matters: Sunk costs on a planning programme that is not progressed can become a write-off, and a finance officer elsewhere would want to know how such costs are recorded and reported.
findings.figures: None stated in the paper.
findings.quote: Considerable officer time and financial resource has already been invested in preparing the emerging Plan.

findings.paper_title: 11. Audit and Governance report Statutory Intervention
findings.headline: The paper identifies a section 27 reimbursement liability: if the Secretary of State prepares or revises the Local Plan in the council's place, the council must repay the expenditure he incurs, with no amount stated.
findings.detail: The report describes the statutory reimbursement as a financial exposure linked to deeper intervention. It also states that there are no new direct financial commitments arising from its recommendations.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or at another council, would want to know that a plan-making failure under section 27 can create a repayable cost to central government, and that the paper gives no estimate of its size.
findings.figures: None stated in the paper.
findings.quote: Section 27 expressly provides for reimbursement to the Secretary of State of expenditure incurred where the Secretary of State undertakes preparation or revision which the authority had failed or omitted to undertake.

findings.committee: Scrutiny Panel - Health and Adult Social Care
findings.paper_title: 7. Q1 2026-27 Council Plan Performance and Finance Report Quarter 1
findings.headline: Capital programme reprofiling has reduced expected borrowing costs and generated additional interest income from higher interest rate environment
findings.detail: Changes to capital programme timelines have resulted in lower expected borrowing costs. The council has benefited from reduced financing cost pressures due to reprofiling of capital spend, alongside increased interest income from rates remaining higher than budget assumptions. This contributed to a corporate budget underspend of £1.1M.
findings.matters: Capital reprofiling affects both the timing and scale of borrowing requirements; current high interest rate environment is creating income benefits that may reverse if rates fall
findings.figures: Corporate budget underspend of £1.1M contributed to by lower borrowing costs and higher interest income
findings.quote: The underspend within Corporate Budgets reflects the impact of lower expected borrowing costs, due to the reprofiling of the capital programme and increased interest income due to rates currently remaining at a higher level than budget.

findings.committee: Scrutiny Panel - Health and Adult Social Care
findings.paper_title: 7. Q1 2026-27 Council Plan Performance and Finance Report Quarter 1
findings.headline: Council managing interest rate uncertainty through short-term borrowing strategy while awaiting long-term rate stability
findings.detail: The council is managing interest rate uncertainty by using short-term borrowing where appropriate while awaiting greater stability in long-term rates. All treasury management activity operates within the approved Treasury Management Strategy and prudential indicators. This approach creates refinancing risk if rates do not stabilise.
findings.matters: Borrowing strategy directly impacts debt servicing costs; short-term borrowing strategy creates refinancing risk if interest rates remain volatile or rise
findings.figures: No specific Q1 borrowing figures disclosed; strategy driven by current rate environment
findings.quote: Given current interest rate uncertainty, the Council has continued to make use of short-term borrowing where appropriate, pending greater stability in long-term rates.

findings.committee: Scrutiny Panel - Health and Adult Social Care
findings.paper_title: 7. Q1 2026-27 Council Plan Performance and Finance Report Quarter 1
findings.headline: Asset disposal programme forecast to outperform target by £1.27M, delivering £4.67M against £3.4M target
findings.detail: The council's asset disposal programme is forecast to deliver £4.672M in capital receipts against an annual target of £3.4M. This represents 37% outperformance and provides additional discretionary capital resources to support the capital programme without requiring additional borrowing.
findings.matters: Capital receipt generation from asset sales is discretionary income that provides financial flexibility and reduces borrowing requirement; outperformance improves headroom
findings.figures: Target £3.4M; forecast delivery £4.672M; outperformance of £1.27M
findings.quote: For the Disposal Programme the year end target for 2026/27 is £3.4m where the work is already currently forecast at £4.672m.

findings.committee: Scrutiny Panel - Health and Adult Social Care
findings.paper_title: 7. Q1 2026-27 Council Plan Performance and Finance Report Quarter 1
findings.headline: Business rates revaluation impact from 1 April 2026 not yet incorporated into MTFP; uncertainty about central government baseline decisions
findings.detail: The full impact of the business rateable valuation changes from 1 April 2026 has not yet been incorporated into the medium-term financial plan because central government is still assessing how these changes will affect business rates baselines for local authorities. Further information is expected in coming months, creating uncertainty for medium-term revenue forecasting.
findings.matters: Business rates are a material and volatile income source; central government baseline decisions directly affect council funding; uncertainty delays financial planning and could expose councils to adverse changes
findings.figures: None provided; timing impact unknown pending central government announcement
findings.quote: The full impact of business rateable valuation changes from 1st April 2026 are yet to be fully incorporated into the MTFP, as central government continues to assess how these changes will impact the business rates baselines for local authorities. Further information is expected in the coming months

findings.committee: Scrutiny Panel - Health and Adult Social Care
findings.paper_title: 7. Q1 2026-27 Council Plan Performance and Finance Report Quarter 1
findings.headline: Housing Benefit subsidy shortfall of £0.25M being covered from earmarked reserves, requiring ongoing monitoring
findings.detail: The council faces ongoing financial risks related to the level of Housing Benefit subsidy available for supported and temporary accommodation. A balanced position is being achieved through drawing £0.25M from earmarked reserves. The council is working to encourage housing providers to register or partner with registered providers, but the subsidy risk requires close monitoring throughout the year.
findings.matters: Structural use of earmarked reserves to cover subsidy shortfalls indicates a funding problem that is not self-correcting and depletes flexibility for other purposes
findings.figures: £0.25M earmarked reserve funding required to balance Housing Subsidy gap
findings.quote: A balanced position is submitted in relation to Housing Subsidy however this is achieved by using £0.25M of EMR funding to balance the gap between costs and funding received. Due to the nature of this area this will need to be monitored closely throughout the year.

findings.committee: Scrutiny Panel - Health and Adult Social Care
findings.paper_title: 7. Q1 2026-27 Council Plan Performance and Finance Report Quarter 1
findings.headline: Employer pension contribution reduced from 19.7% to 14.3% following actuarial revaluation, releasing £1.5M
findings.detail: The formal actuarial revaluation by Hymans Robertson of the East Riding Pension Fund employer contributions has reduced the primary rate from 19.7% to 14.3%. This reduction is enabling the council to remove the secondary pension contribution of £1.5M, providing structural relief to the baseline budget position.
findings.matters: Pension cost reductions are structural improvements that strengthen the underlying budget position and reduce reliance on contingency or reserves for future years
findings.figures: Primary contribution reduced from 19.7% to 14.3%; £1.5M secondary pension contribution removal for next 3 years
findings.quote: Following the final actuarial valuation of pension contribution requirements for the next 3 financial years, the Council will remove the secondary pension contribution of £1.5M, this will further aid in the offset of the demand led service pressures.

findings.committee: Scrutiny Panel - Health and Adult Social Care
findings.paper_title: 7. Q1 2026-27 Council Plan Performance and Finance Report Quarter 1
findings.headline: Unprecedented EHCP demand and high-cost adult care placements exceed budget assumptions in both children's and adult social care
findings.detail: Children's Services faces unprecedented demand for Education, Health and Care Plans alongside challenges in children in care numbers. Adult Social Care is experiencing rising demand including high-cost placements above the level assumed during budget setting. Both services are reviewing cost package reviews and demand management options but remain forecast to overspend.
findings.matters: Social care demand is demand-led and difficult to control; exceeding assumptions at Q1 signals risk for the rest of the year and questions whether MTFP assumptions are realistic
findings.figures: Adult Services budget £76.1M, forecast outturn £78.2M (£2.1M overspend); Children's Services also experiencing overspend driven by EHCP and children in care pressures
findings.quote: In Children's Services, despite the continued positive transformation, challenges around Children in Care numbers and unprecedented demand for Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) have changed the assumptions applied when setting the balanced budget, resulting in a revised forecast position. Furthermore, Adult Social Care is also experiencing rising demand, including high-cost placements above the level assumed during budget setting.

findings.committee: Scrutiny Panel - Health and Adult Social Care
findings.paper_title: 7. Q1 2026-27 Council Plan Performance and Finance Report Quarter 1
findings.headline: Full year revenue overspend of £1.8M forecast at Q1 driven by social care demand
findings.detail: The council forecasts a full year overspend of £1.8M at the end of Q1. This is being mitigated through release of £1.4M service contingency and removal of £1.5M secondary pension contribution. Both mitigating actions are deployed but the underlying demand pressures remain significant, indicating residual financial risk through the year.
findings.matters: A material overspend at Q1 indicates whether demand assumptions underpinning the MTFP remain valid; the mitigation strategy matters for assessing financial resilience and reserve depletion risk
findings.figures: £1.8M full year overspend forecast; £1.4M contingency release; £1.5M pension contribution reduction
findings.quote: Rising social care demand continues to place significant pressure on the overall financial position of the Council. As a result, a full year overspend of £1.8M is forecast at Q1.

findings.headline: Investment strategy prioritises security over yield, holding 11-day average maturity investments at AA credit rating and 4.02% return, below market average
findings.detail: The council's investment strategy is deliberately cautious. Average maturity is 11 days (vs 535-day sector average) and weighted average credit rating is AA (vs target of A-). Average return achieved was 4.02%, marginally below peer average of 3.72%. This reflects post-Bail-in regulatory environment where the S151 Officer prioritises elimination of credit risk through lower cash balances over yield optimisation. The council holds less cash (£12m average vs £98m peer average) and accepts below-market returns as trade-off for security.
findings.matters: This is a stated policy choice, not a constraint; it shows conservative risk management but also potential forgone revenue; peer councils use higher yields and longer maturities to support services; lenders assess whether this approach reflects prudence or opportunity cost.
findings.figures: 11 days average maturity, 4.02% return, AA credit rating, £12m average balance held
findings.quote: NELC hold less cash. Average balance £12m vs £98m average for the Group… NELC invest for shorter periods. Only 10 days vs 535 days on average across the Group… NELC take less risk than the Group collectively… NELC deliver slightly below average return. 3.69% vs 3.72% average return for the Group

findings.headline: Temporary borrowing required to fund SEND deficits during 2025-26, offsetting £25m capital programme slippage benefit
findings.detail: The report states that the £25m benefit from capital programme slippage 'was partially offset by temporary borrowing required to fund SEND deficits.' This indicates underlying revenue pressure in a statutory service (special educational needs and disabilities provision). The amount is not quantified in the outturn, suggesting it may be cash-flow timing related, but signals ongoing structural SEND funding issues in the council's budget.
findings.matters: SEND deficits are a sector-wide pressure affecting many councils; temporary borrowing for revenue purposes is generally expected to reverse but may indicate structural underfunding; lenders track SEND as a key risk area for medium-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Amount not quantified; described as 'temporary borrowing'
findings.quote: Entering 2025-26, period end borrowing levels were forecast to be around £203.3m. Actual borrowing at year end stood at £178.1m (£25m lower than forecast). This was primarily due to slippage of schemes within the Capital Programme, although this was partially offset by temporary borrowing required to fund SEND deficits.

findings.headline: No changes made to Treasury Management Strategy Statement during year despite two major periods of financial market volatility (US tariffs April 2025, Iran conflict February 2026)
findings.detail: The TMSS approved in February 2025 required no mid-year revisions despite significant market volatility. The S151 Officer reports 'the Strategy did its job in protecting public funds whilst allowing sufficient flexibility to cope with exceptional operational demands.' This indicates either robust policy design or a deliberate choice to maintain steady course rather than react tactically to short-term volatility.
findings.matters: Stability of policy provides governance clarity; however, absence of tactical adjustments during 11 percentage points of base rate movement and commodity price shocks may indicate conservative hedging or opportunity cost.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: There were no in-year policy changes to the TMSS – pleasing to note in the face of challenging economic circumstances; the Strategy did its job in protecting public funds whilst allowing sufficient flexibility to cope with exceptional operational demands.

findings.headline: Council anticipates borrowing £114m over next few years as capital programme resumes and internal cash reserves deplete
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer notes that 'the Authority has an increasing CFR over the next four years due to the capital programme, and as investments reduce will need to borrow up to £114m over the next few years.' Further borrowing is anticipated during 2026-27. This signals substantial future refinancing requirement across multiple years, with timing and cost dependent on interest rate path.
findings.matters: This quantifies forward funding requirement and refinancing risk; the scale (£114m) and horizon (next 4 years) signal significant market access need; timing of execution will affect debt costs and the council's rate-lock strategy.
findings.figures: £114m cumulative future borrowing need, borrowing in 2026-27 to follow
findings.quote: The Authority has an increasing CFR over the next four years due to the capital programme, and as investments reduce will need to borrow up to £114m over the next few years.

findings.headline: Debt affordability ratio came in at 5.98% of revenue budget for 2025-26 but projected to rise to 9.43% by 2027-28, approaching prudential ceiling
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs (net of investment income) to net revenue stream was 5.98% in 2025-26, well below the original estimate of 8.83%, due to capital programme slippage and higher investment income. However, this metric is projected to deteriorate sharply: rising to 7.84% in 2026-27 and 9.43% in 2027-28. The 10% prudential guideline for affordability begins to tighten financial headroom. The improvement in 2025-26 is temporary and reversal is expected as capital programme executes.
findings.matters: This is the key affordability metric tracked by finance directors and lenders; the current year improvement masks structural tightening as deferred capital spending flows through; approaching 10% ceiling constrains future spending flexibility.
findings.figures: 2025-26 actual 5.98% vs 8.83% estimate; 2026-27 forecast 7.84%; 2027-28 forecast 9.43%
findings.quote: The percentage of the Council's income required to service its net debt came in below 2025/26 projections due to a combination of slippage in the capital programme and a much higher than anticipated income from investments due to the availability of higher market rates.

findings.headline: Council maintained deliberately under-borrowed position of £58.4m below Capital Financing Requirement (£236.5m CFR vs £178.1m borrowing)
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement (the underlying measure of capital borrowing need) was £236.5m but gross external borrowing was only £178.1m. This £58.4m gap reflects deliberate under-borrowing strategy using internal cash reserves to defer expensive long-term borrowing while rates remain elevated. This approach has trade-offs: it defers costs but uses up cash buffers and creates reinvestment risk when balances must eventually be rebuilt.
findings.matters: Under-borrowing is a tactical timing strategy with medium-term risk: it reduces current-year debt costs but locks in higher refinancing requirement later; lenders track whether councils can sustain this position or face forced borrowing at inopportune rates.
findings.figures: Under-borrowed position £58.4m, CFR £236.5m, external borrowing £178.1m, total debt £184.7m
findings.quote: During 2025/26, the Council maintained an under-borrowed position. This meant that the capital borrowing need, (the Capital Financing Requirement), was not fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Council's reserves, balances and cash flow was used as an interim measure. This strategy was prudent as investment returns are typically below borrowing rates and minimising counterparty risk on placing investments also needed to be considered.

findings.headline: Council arranged 26 short-term loans from other local authorities totalling £123.7m at rates 4.25–5.10%, avoiding long-term PWLB borrowing despite elevated costs
findings.detail: The council did not arrange any new long-term PWLB borrowing during 2025-26, instead executing 26 separate short-term loans with other councils and fire services, maturing within 2 months to 16 months. Rates on these deals reflected local authority lending market conditions tightened by liquidity pressures from Section 114 notices in the sector and SEND funding formula impacts. This strategy defers expensive long-term funding but creates refinancing concentration risk and maturity clustering.
findings.matters: Heavy reliance on LA lending market (91% of new short-term borrowing) creates concentration risk; sector liquidity tightening is a warning indicator for future access and pricing; all these loans mature within 16 months and will need replacement or refinancing.
findings.figures: 26 deals totalling £123.7m, rates 4.25–5.10%, maturity range 2 months to 16 months; PWLB borrowing £11.2m of the total
findings.quote: In the local authority market, rates reflected liquidity issues with many regular lenders reducing their exposure on the back of a combination of Section 114 Notices issued in the sector, Schools SEND Funding Formula issues removing capacity and competitive rates available elsewhere.

findings.headline: Treasury operations generated £3m surplus for frontline services: £1.3m investment income above budget plus £1.7m borrowing cost underspend
findings.detail: Investment income came in £1.3m above budget due to higher market rates during an elevated rate environment. Interest costs on borrowing came in £1.3m under original budget at £6.93m. Of the £1.7m borrowing underspend, £0.5m was allocated to a new Debt Financing Reserve to build resilience against future higher cost of debt. The combined £3m surplus supports frontline service delivery.
findings.matters: Treasury surpluses fund services without raising borrowing or tax; investment income is market-driven (timing dependent) while borrowing savings reflect deferral strategy; the reserve allocation shows forward planning for the projected rate environment.
findings.figures: £1.3m investment surplus, £1.7m borrowing underspend, £6.93m actual interest paid, £0.5m allocated to Debt Financing Reserve
findings.quote: Higher investment returns, even with our cautious approach, has generated surplus income (above budget) of £1.3m during the period, income which is available to fund frontline services. Underspend on borrowing provided another £1.7m for distribution, including £0.5m allocated to a Debt Financing Reserve to provide resilience against the impact of potential higher cost of debt in future years.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure slipped 34% (£37.3m) from £108.4m budget to £71.1m outturn, deferring borrowing requirement into 2026-27
findings.detail: The council's capital programme came in significantly under-spent. This slippage was the primary driver of actual borrowing (£178.1m) being £25m lower than forecast (£203.3m). The deferred capital spending is expected to flow through 2026-27, creating a front-loaded borrowing requirement for the coming year.
findings.matters: Large capital slippage affects cash flow timing and borrowing requirement sequencing; it defers debt costs in the current year but concentrates them in future years; lenders and peer finance directors track whether slippage is routine variation or signals delivery risk.
findings.figures: Budget £108.4m, outturn £71.1m, slippage £37.3m (34%)
findings.quote: Entering 2025-26, period end borrowing levels were forecast to be around £203.3m. Actual borrowing at year end stood at £178.1m (£25m lower than forecast). This was primarily due to slippage of schemes within the Capital Programme, although this was partially offset by temporary borrowing required to fund SEND deficits.

findings.headline: £10m LOBO loan called and repaid without penalty; £1m LOBO remaining outstanding to 2035
findings.detail: A Lender Option Borrower Option (LOBO) loan of £10m was called during the year and the council exercised its repayment right at par value without penalty. One smaller £1m LOBO loan remains outstanding with maturity in 2035. LOBO calls are significant refinancing events that trigger replacement funding requirements.
findings.matters: LOBO repayments eliminate future rate-reset risk on that tranche but represent cash refinancing need; lenders and peer councils track LOBO market activity as indicator of rate environment and council refinancing exposure.
findings.figures: £10m repaid, £1m remaining to 2035
findings.quote: A further Lender Option, Borrower Option (LOBO) loan (£10m) was called and duly repaid without penalty during the period. This leaves one smaller (£1m) LOBO remaining outstanding with an ultimate maturity date of 2035.

findings.paper_title: 9. Highway and Transport Capital Programme Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Winter 2026 caused significant pothole formation surge; Council allocating £168k innovation budget for new prevention and response methods
findings.detail: Prolonged winter freezing followed by sustained rainfall significantly accelerated surface deterioration and pothole formation. The council is responding with a £168,210 innovation programme to develop and trial new technologies and methods for pothole prevention and response. Further scrutiny review of equipment trials is scheduled before any permanent implementation of new working methods.
findings.matters: Finance officers at councils facing similar pothole pressures would want to know how peers are addressing the issue. This shows one council responding to emerging service demand through efficiency innovation rather than requesting additional funding.
findings.figures: £168,210 allocated to preventative maintenance technology and innovation trial
findings.quote: Winter 2026 caused a significant increase in pothole formation and repairs on local highways. Prolonged freezing conditions, followed by sustained heavy rainfall, have significantly accelerated surface deterioration and pothole formation.

findings.paper_title: 9. Highway and Transport Capital Programme Cabinet Report
findings.headline: £17.4m highways capital programme is fully funded and requires no additional borrowing beyond that already reflected in Council's Treasury Management and Capital Strategies
findings.detail: The 2026/27 programme totals £17,438,155. Funding comprises £4.516m Highways Maintenance grant, £7.317m Local Transport Grant, £5.034m carried forward from 2025/26, and £400,000 corporate allocation. The council explicitly confirms no new borrowing is required for delivery.
findings.matters: For lenders and peer finance officers, this demonstrates the council is managing a substantial capital programme within available resources without increasing debt levels.
findings.figures: £17,438,155 total; £4.516m Highways Maintenance grant; £7.317m Local Transport Grant; £5.034m carried forward; £400,000 corporate allocation
findings.quote: The programme is fully funded within the Council's approved Capital Investment Programme and does not require any additional borrowing beyond that already reflected within the Council's Treasury Management and Capital Strategies.

findings.headline: Debt interest costs budgeted at £9.68m in 2026/27 on average debt of £220m at 4.40% average rate
findings.detail: The council budgets debt interest payments of £9.680m for 2026/27, based on forecast average debt portfolio of £220m at 4.40% average interest rate. Investment income is budgeted at just £0.350m, creating a net financing cost that reflects the council's position as a significant borrower in an elevated rate environment.
findings.matters: High debt service cost relative to minimal investment income shows limited reserve offset; debt costs are substantially above historic levels and create significant revenue commitment.
findings.figures: Debt interest budget £9.680m; investment income budget £0.350m; average debt £220m; average rate 4.40%
findings.quote: The budget for investment income in 2026/27 is £0.350 million. The budget for debt interest paid in 2026/27 is £9.680 million, based on an average debt portfolio of £220 million at an average interest rate of 4.40%.

findings.headline: Limit on long-term investments reduced to £2m, signalling defensive positioning and LOBO hedging preparation
findings.detail: The council has tightened its limit on investments beyond 366 days to £2m for 2026/27 (substantially reduced from prior years). The council explicitly states this reduction is to: (1) preserve flexibility for a potential 'defeasement' transaction to hedge remaining LOBO loan risk if market conditions warrant, and (2) maintain flexibility to lock in higher rates without constraining liquidity.
findings.matters: More conservative investment positioning indicates awareness of refinancing risk on remaining LOBO loans and desire to maintain tactical borrowing flexibility during uncertain rate environment.
findings.figures: Non-specified investment limit for long-term principal beyond 366 days: £2m (2026/27, reduced)
findings.quote: *Reduced limit to cover 1) option of 'defeasement' transaction on remaining LOBO and 2) flexibility to lock in higher rates without materially impacting on overall liquidity.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement rises 16% in one year from £251.7m to £292.2m
findings.detail: The council's underlying borrowing need (CFR) has grown from £251.7m (forecast at 31 March 2026) to £292.2m in 2026/27, a £40.5m increase in one year. This is driven primarily by the capital expenditure budget increasing 42% from £80.0m to £113.7m, creating the bulk of the new £141m borrowing requirement.
findings.matters: Rapid capital programme growth at time of elevated interest rates and constrained finances significantly increases debt service burden and revenue impact; sustainability dependent on continued capital delivery.
findings.figures: CFR growth £251.7m to £292.2m; capital expenditure £80.0m to £113.7m (42% increase)
findings.quote: The Authority has an increasing CFR due to the capital programme and will therefore need to borrow in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Short-term borrowing strategy continues to avoid peak rates, with explicit timing risk documented
findings.detail: Rather than lock in long-term borrowing at current elevated rates (5.2-5.8% for 10-50 year PWLB), the council plans to continue using short-term borrowing and refinance regularly as rates are expected to fall. The S151 Officer explicitly identifies the risk: if rates do not fall as anticipated, the council may miss the opportunity to lock in lower rates.
findings.matters: This is an active interest rate timing bet; failure would result in unnecessarily high debt costs during period when rates may plateau or reverse.
findings.figures: Current PWLB rates 5yr 4.50%, 10yr 5.20%, 25yr 5.80%, 50yr 5.60%; Bank Rate forecast 3.25% by March 2027
findings.quote: Given the elevated rates seen in 2025 we plan to continue using short-term borrowing to meet our need. This strategy, whilst still sound, isn't without risk. Risk that a temporary decline in rates is missed while we wait for clearer signs of trajectory

findings.headline: Treasury function expanded to Combined Authority and Freeport; capacity flagged as ongoing concern
findings.detail: The treasury team now manages borrowing and investment for the council plus two additional entities (Combined Authority and Freeport). The S151 Officer reports the team has coped with this expanded scope despite personnel changes, but has flagged capacity as remaining under close review, echoing concerns raised in the 2009 Public Interest Report following Iceland bank crisis.
findings.matters: Treasury staff capacity constraints create operational execution risk; stretched teams increase likelihood of error in high-value transactions. Historical precedent shows this was previously a material weakness.
findings.figures: Treasury function expanded to three entities (council plus two); capacity flagged as key issue post-Iceland
findings.quote: The Treasury function has coped admirably with this demanding operational environment despite several personnel changes, supporting not only NELC's treasury management but also that of the new Combined Authority and the Freeport entity. Capacity, a key issue in the 2009 Public Interest Report (post-Iceland), remains under close review.

findings.headline: Negative reserves driven by SEND pressures are permitted only until 2028
findings.detail: The council holds negative reserves resulting from Special Educational Needs and Disabilities cost pressures. Government rules currently permit this, but only until 2028. This time-limited permission is forcing the council to take on additional new borrowing to manage cash flow rather than using reserves to fund capital schemes.
findings.matters: Hard deadline of 2028 means deficit position must be resolved within three years; interim period forces additional debt funding and higher costs. Unresolved, this creates sustainability risk.
findings.figures: Negative reserves permitted until 31 March 2028
findings.quote: Negative reserve positions brought about by SEND pressures, whilst permitted until 2028, have manifested themselves in additional cash requirement, managed through lower overall balances and new borrowing.

findings.headline: £141m of new borrowing required over three years to fund capital programme and debt maturity
findings.detail: The council forecasts it will need up to £141m of new borrowing across 2026/27-2028/29, comprising both the capital programme expansion and £62m of existing loan maturities. Capital expenditure is rising sharply from £80.0m (current forecast) to £113.7m in 2026/27, and external debt is forecast to grow from £185.8m to £226.4m.
findings.matters: Large refinancing requirement at structurally elevated interest rates (4.50-5.80% for PWLB) significantly increases debt service costs and revenue burden; refinancing risk concentrated in period when rates remain uncertain.
findings.figures: £141m new borrowing required 2026/27-2028/29; capital expenditure £80.0m to £113.7m; existing maturities £62m; external borrowing £185.8m to £226.4m
findings.quote: In total the Authority will need up to £141m of new borrowing assuming the Capital Programme is delivered as forecast over the next three years.

findings.headline: Auditor's Value for Money qualification lifted, restoring market borrowing access
findings.detail: The council had been unable to access commercial borrowing from banks and insurance companies due to an audit qualification on its Statement of Accounts. Removal of this qualification in 2026 restores access to these lenders, providing greater flexibility in sourcing the substantial new borrowing the council requires.
findings.matters: Loss and restoration of market access directly affects which lenders will advance funds and on what terms; material to refinancing strategy during a period of significant new borrowing needs.
findings.figures: n/a
findings.quote: One positive change for 2026/27 is the removal our Auditor's Value For Money qualification in our Statement of Accounts. This restores our access to the wider Market (banks/insurers etc) which can offer us more flexible borrowing arrangements.

findings.paper_title: 5. Budget and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Business rates scheme changes in 2026/27 introduce new multipliers for retail, hospitality and high-value properties, with uncertain impact
findings.detail: Three-yearly revaluation of rateable values takes effect 1 April 2026 alongside introduction of new multipliers for Retail, Hospitality & Leisure (RHL) and high-value properties over £500k, replacing previous reliefs. Changes managed through transitional reliefs. Council adding additional 15% relief for eligible pubs and live music venues. New scheme coincides with already-declining collection performance.
findings.matters: Uncertain impact on yield. Combined with declining collection rates, represents risk to business rates income forecast.
findings.figures: High-value property threshold £500k; 15% additional relief for eligible pubs and venues; new baseline reset
findings.quote: This includes the regular three-yearly revaluation of business rateable values and the introduction of new multipliers for Retail, Hospitality & Leisure (RHL) and high-value properties (over £500k), which will replace previous reliefs in the RHL sector.

findings.paper_title: 5. Budget and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Council using capital receipts flexibility to fund revenue transformation costs, a non-sustainable financing source
findings.detail: As in prior year, council is applying government's flexibility to use capital receipts towards funding revenue costs of transformation. This is a one-off financing mechanism that cannot continue once capital receipts are exhausted or needed for capital investment. It helps balance revenue budgets now but masks underlying gap.
findings.matters: Non-sustainable financing source masks structural budget challenge. Reduces capital available for investment. When exhausted, budget gap re-emerges.
findings.figures: Amount not specified in this section
findings.quote: As in 2025/26, the Council intends to utilise the Government's flexibility to apply capital receipts towards funding the revenue costs of transformation and change.

findings.paper_title: 5. Budget and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Children's services rated Good in July 2025 ILACS inspection, with Outstanding leadership
findings.detail: Recent Ofsted improvement grading follows restructured staffing, new sufficiency strategy to reduce reliance on high-cost external placements, and new case management system. Council plans continued improvement. This is genuine positive movement in a historically pressured service area, which should moderate cost growth going forward.
findings.matters: Children's services was a major cost pressure and audit concern; improvement is material risk reduction for future years. Cost management should improve if improvement trajectory continues.
findings.figures: July 2025 rating; Good service, Outstanding leadership
findings.quote: The July 2025 ILACS inspection, where children's services were graded as Good, with Outstanding leadership.

findings.paper_title: 5. Budget and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Three-year settlement with Fair Funding Review benefit phased in at one-third per year through 2028/29
findings.detail: Settlement confirms 6.1% cash increase in funding overall, but this masks uneven distribution. Fair Funding Review (FFR) allocates only one-third of increased funding each year until full amount received in 2028/29. This provides medium-term planning visibility but creates cliff risk if settlement does not extend beyond 2029.
findings.matters: Clarity is good but dependent on continuation beyond 2028/29. Council must plan for potential loss of phased FFR benefit if multi-year settlement not extended.
findings.figures: 6.1% cash increase overall; one-third FFR benefit allocated each of 2026/27, 2027/28, 2028/29
findings.quote: However, the full benefit of the FFR will be phased in over the settlement period, with approximately one third of the increased funding allocated each year until the full amount is received in 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: 5. Budget and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Council raising council tax and social care precept at maximum permitted levels, limiting future revenue-raising headroom
findings.detail: Council is applying 2.99% increase to base council tax (at 3% referendum limit) and 2% Adult Social Care precept (maximum available). Combined these raise £80.2M core council tax and £16.6M ASC precept for 2026/27. Council tax base growth is minimal: only 8.9 band D equivalent new properties yielding £17k. By maximizing current-year levers, council has limited flexibility for revenue growth in future.
findings.matters: Council tax and precepts are now ceiling income sources for this council. Future budget gaps cannot be filled from council tax; must come from spending cuts or other income.
findings.figures: £80.2M core council tax; £16.6M ASC precept; 2.99% increase plus 2% precept; tax base growth £17k on minimal property growth
findings.quote: The ASC precept will raise a total of £16.6M in 2026/27 which will mitigate increased social care demand pressures.

findings.paper_title: 5. Budget and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Adult social care demand and complexity continue to increase, requiring sustained transformation focus
findings.detail: Council identifies adult social care as the key area of demand and cost pressure going forward: both volume and complexity of need are rising. This is being addressed through transformation plans, but transformation is not guaranteed to match pace of demand. ASC is now funded partly through precept (£16.6M from 2% social care precept in 2026/27) and partly from core grant allocation.
findings.matters: Ongoing cost driver that rises regardless of council actions. Complexity particularly matters as it increases cost per case. A finance director must track whether transformation is keeping pace.
findings.figures: ASC precept raising £16.6M in 2026/27; core allocation to be confirmed
findings.quote: Continued transformation and targeted change will be essential to ensure the Council achieves the right outcomes and maintains financial sustainability over the medium term, particularly in Adult Social Care, where both demand and complexity are increasing.

findings.paper_title: 5. Budget and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Council increasing reserve contributions in 2026/27 to buffer transformation period and ongoing uncertainty
findings.detail: Council is building reserves above normal levels, explicitly stating this reflects the 'current period of transformation and ongoing uncertainty.' This is a precautionary measure signalling the council's own assessment of risk in delivering its plans—acknowledging execution risk exists even as it plans for success.
findings.matters: Reserve building can smooth shocks but also signals underlying uncertainty. A council building reserves while claiming a balanced budget is hedging its bets on plan delivery.
findings.figures: Increase in net reserve contributions proposed but amount not specified in this section
findings.quote: The proposed increase in net contributions to reserves for 2026/27 reflects the current period of transformation and ongoing uncertainty.

findings.paper_title: 5. Budget and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Business rates collection fell during 2025/26; forecasting challenging in current economic environment
findings.detail: Collection performance was below prior-year levels at mid-2025/26. With businesses facing rising costs and smaller firms particularly affected, forecasting is difficult. Council maintains Business Rates Reserve to smooth volatility. Rates are material income: approximately £54.6M forecast for 2026/27, around 25% of total revenue funding.
findings.matters: Declining collection is a cash risk that may require reserve draws. Business rates are the second-largest income source after council tax.
findings.figures: £54.6M forecast 2026/27; collection rate challenged; reserve held to manage swings
findings.quote: Collection performance for Business Rates was slightly reduced against previous years as at the mid-point of 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: 5. Budget and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Budget is balanced for 2026/27-2028/29 but dependent on successful delivery of transformation plans
findings.detail: The council explicitly states the balanced position is conditional: 'not without risk and is dependant on the successful delivery of ambitious business and transformation plans.' Transformation is particularly needed in Adult Social Care (demand and complexity rising) and Children's Services (though recently rated Good). The budget cannot balance without execution of planned changes.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance directors need to distinguish between structural balance and balance dependent on uncertain future delivery. This budget is the latter.
findings.figures: 2026/27-2028/29 budget periods affected
findings.quote: Both the 2026/27 budget and future years are balanced, but this position is not without risk and is dependant on the successful delivery of ambitious business and transformation plans to secure long-term financial sustainability.

findings.headline: Q1 2025/26 revenue forecast £1.5m overspend indicates underlying demand-led spending pressures not fully resolved
findings.detail: The council recovered from Q3 2024/25 forecast overspend of £0.9m to a balanced outturn through management action on Children's Services including staffing reconfiguration, renewed sufficiency strategy to reduce high-cost external placements, and new case management system implementation. However Q1 2025/26 forecast presented to Cabinet in August 2025 shows £1.5m projected overspend against budget. Early-year overspend suggests the underlying structural cost drivers in demand-led services (particularly children's and social care) remain unresolved despite 2024/25 recovery measures.
findings.matters: The return to overspend forecast in the new financial year, despite recovery actions taken in 2024/25, signals that spending pressures remain structural rather than one-off. Early-year overspends typically cascade through the financial year. This is material context for lenders and peer councils managing similar social care cost pressures.
findings.figures: Q3 2024/25 forecast overspend £0.9m; 2024/25 outturn balanced; Q1 2025/26 forecast overspend £1.5m
findings.quote: The 2025/26 Quarter 1 forecast revenue position, presented to Cabinet in August 2025 has the Council forecasting an overspend of £1.5m against budget, it does not currently indicate a significant weakness in the Council's arrangements.

findings.headline: Unqualified audit opinion issued 22 December 2025 on 2024/25 financial statements with no material misstatements identified
findings.detail: The auditors issued an unqualified opinion on the financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025, confirming they give a true and fair view without qualification. Draft accounts were received on 30 June 2025 (ahead of statutory deadline) and assessed as of good quality with comprehensive working papers. Three significant audit risks (management override, valuation of land and buildings/investment properties, pension valuation) were satisfactorily addressed with no material issues. Auditors encountered no significant difficulties and noted full cooperation from management.
findings.matters: An unqualified audit opinion confirms the reliability of financial statements for assessing the council's financial position. Against the backdrop of DSG deficits, children's services investment, and staffing challenges, a clean audit indicates sound financial governance and accounting practices.
findings.figures: Audit opinion issued 22 December 2025; draft accounts submitted 30 June 2025; three significant risks all satisfactorily addressed with no material misstatements
findings.quote: Our audit report, issued on 22 December 2025 gave an unqualified opinion on the financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant outturn overspend of £7.95m driven by High Needs Block with statutory override protection extended to March 2028
findings.detail: The 2024/25 DSG outturn shows an overspend of £7.95m, primarily driven by High Needs Block pressures. This is part of a cumulative DSG deficit growing across the sector. The Government's statutory override (which defers incorporation of DSG deficits into councils' useable reserves) was extended from its original March 2026 expiry to March 2028. On expiry, the cumulative deficit must be incorporated into reserves with severe impact on sustainability. Auditors acknowledge this is a major national issue but stress the council must work with partners on comprehensive mitigation planning.
findings.matters: DSG deficits represent one of the most significant structural financial challenges in English local government. The override extension provides time, but only to March 2028. After that, the cumulative deficit becomes a direct liability on reserves. Lenders and peer councils are monitoring how this sector-wide issue will be resolved.
findings.figures: £7.95m DSG outturn overspend 2024/25; statutory override extended to 31 March 2028 (from 31 March 2026); described by auditors as a major national issue impacting local authorities across the country
findings.quote: On expiry of the override, the Council would need to incorporate the cumulative deficit in its useable reserves, which would have a significantly detrimental impact to the Council's financial sustainability.

findings.headline: OFSTED reassessment of children's services from Inadequate to Good in July 2025 removes prior significant governance weakness
findings.detail: The council faced a prior-year significant weakness following OFSTED's October 2021 Inadequate rating for children's services, citing weaknesses in assessment, planning and decision-making. A full OFSTED inspection in July 2025 rated children's services as Good overall and Outstanding for impact of leaders on social work practice. The auditors are satisfied the improvement was evident throughout 2024/25 based on interim monitoring, and confirm the significant weakness can now be lifted. The council invested significantly through flexible capital receipts and earmarked reserves to fund the service transformation.
findings.matters: Removal of a significant governance weakness materially improves the council's risk profile. For peer finance directors, demonstrates that targeted investment in service transformation can address inspection findings and institutional risk.
findings.figures: OFSTED inspection July 2025; prior 2021 rating Inadequate; July 2025 rating Good overall and Outstanding for leadership impact
findings.quote: In July 2025 OFSTED completed an Inspection of North East Lincolnshire's local authority children's services, and has now reported its findings. The overall assessment was Good in all areas, except for the impact of leaders on social work practice with children and families, which was rated as Outstanding.

news_drafts.headline: North East Lincolnshire forecasts £1.8m revenue overspend driven by Education, Health and Care Plan and adult social care demand
news_drafts.lead: North East Lincolnshire Council expects to overspend its budget by £1.8M by the end of the financial year, driven by unprecedented demand for Education, Health and Care Plans for children and high-cost adult social care placements that exceed what was assumed during budget setting. The council is mitigating the pressure through releasing £1.4M from service contingency and removing a secondary pension contribution of £1.5M, following an actuarial revaluation that reduced the council's employer pension contribution rate from 19.7% to 14.3%. Both mitigating actions are deployed. The scrutiny panel was told the underlying demand pressures remain significant, indicating residual financial risk through the year. Adult Social Care alone is forecast to overspend by £2.1M against a budget of £76.1M.
news_drafts.paper_title: 7. Q1 2026-27 Council Plan Performance and Finance Report Quarter 1

news_drafts.headline: North East Lincolnshire ended 2025-26 with borrowing of £178.1m, £25m below its forecast
news_drafts.lead:
North East Lincolnshire Council finished the 2025-26 financial year with borrowing of £178.1m, £25m lower than the £203.3m it had forecast at the start of the year. The figures are in the council's treasury management outturn report. Treasury management is how a council borrows, invests its spare cash and manages the risks of both, and outturn means the actual figures once a year has ended.

The report says the lower figure was primarily due to slippage in the capital programme, the council's planned spending on things that last, such as buildings, roads and equipment. Schemes within the programme did not progress as fast as planned, so borrowing for them came in below the forecast.

The gap would have been wider without spending on special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) provision. The report says the benefit from slippage was partially offset by temporary borrowing required to fund SEND deficits. It does not put a figure on that temporary borrowing, so the paper does not show how much of the £25m it absorbed.
